newsitem.title: FRANCE: No miracle cure for French unemployment rate - poll.
newsitem.headline: No miracle cure for French unemployment rate - poll.

text.p: The new French government's pledge to cut unemployment is seen as having little impact with economists expecting the jobless rate to stay above 12 percent this year and next, a Reuter poll of 23 economists published on Wednesday showed.

According to median forecasts the unemployment rate was seen sticking at the current rate of 12.5 percent until the end of 1997 then gradually declining during 1998 to reach 12.1 percent by the fourth quarter.
The forecasts were collected between July 9 and July 16.

The unemployment predictions were lower than in a previous Reuter survey conducted in April, but most economists said this was because of a recent revision to the jobless data by national statistics institute INSEE.
INSEE said on June 27 the April unemployment rate, based on International Labour Organisation (ILO) criteria, had been revised down to 12.5 percent from a record 12.8 percent.
The revision followed INSEE's annual labour market review which is carried out in March and serves as the basis for monthly jobless rate calculations for the following year.

Despite the Socialist's campaign pledges to make jobs a priority most said the government's conflicting goal of trimming public deficits to get in shape for European monetary union had effectively postponed an assault on the jobless queues.

"The prospects for job creation are getting more distant. The scope for state sector jobs is very limited. The real source has got to be the private sector and all (the new government) has done is threaten to increase unit wage costs and clobber (companies) for tax," Iain Lindsay at Credit Lyonnais said.
Some economists, however, said there could be scope for some surprises, not necessarily on job creation, but on the size of the labour force, which would also trim the jobless rate.

"It depends on the labour force and it is extremely difficult to understand. It is so high and so far from the demographic trend I wouldn't be surprised if we had some surprises," Eric Chaney at Morgan Stanley said.

He said an expected increase in the French labour force of about 180,000 this year was far bigger than a more typical rise of around 110,000 or 120,000 and a reversal of the trend next year could cut the unemployment rate.

Other economists said there were signs of a move towards more part-time and flexible work practices in France which would allow firms to respond more quickly to any acceleration in activity, although some were more optimistic than others.
